content: Amaranth, also known as FD&C Red No. 2 or by its identifier 16185, is a dark red to purple azo dye that was historically used as a food coloring agent and in cosmetic products. However, since 1976, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has banned its use due to concerns that it may be a carcinogen. The dye is typically available in the form of a trisodium salt and appears as a reddish-brown to dark red or purple water-soluble powder. It decomposes at 120°C without melting. When dissolved in water, it exhibits a maximum absorption wavelength of approximately 520 nm. Amaranth is synthesized from coal tar and is classified as an anionic dye. It can be applied to a variety of materials, including natural and synthetic fibers, leather, paper, and phenol-formaldehyde resins. As a food additive, it was assigned the E number E123. In 1969, Soviet researchers discovered that prolonged exposure to Red Dye No. 2, even at the low concentrations typically found in food products, caused cancer in laboratory animals. Following these findings, the FDA conducted its own studies based on the Soviet research protocols, but the results were inconclusive. Despite this, the FDA proceeded to ban FD&C Red No. 2 in 1976. Subsequently, other dyes such as FD&C Red No. 3 (erythrosine), FD&C Red No. 40, and Allura Red AC were introduced as replacements for the decertified color.
